opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing I look for is whether the task actually matters, whether it's connected to real value in the world. In the earlier days of agent research, a lot of the environments were games or synthetic tasks. They were clean and easy to evaluate, but there was a gap between doing well on them and doing something people actually care about. So when we built WebShop, and later when people worked on things like SWE-bench or tau-bench, the motivation was to get closer to real usage: shopping on a website, fixing a real GitHub issue, talking to a customer while following a policy.

The second thing is that the task should be hard in the right way. Not hard because of some trick, but because it needs the abilities we think are important for agents: reasoning over long horizons, using tools, dealing with noisy information, interacting with humans. Ideally, when a model gets better at the task, it means it has gotten better at something general, not that it has overfit to a quirk of the benchmark.

Third, it has to be scalable and evaluable. You want automatic, reliable reward or evaluation, so you can run many experiments and compare methods fairly. If evaluation needs a human every time, it's hard to make fast progress. Good environments often have this property: the task is complex and open-ended, but checking the result is relatively simple. Like with code, you can run the unit tests.

And I think increasingly, especially now that we're in what I call the "second half" of AI, defining the right task and evaluation is maybe more important than designing a new method. In the first half, people took benchmarks as given and competed on methods. Now the general recipe, large-scale pretraining plus reinforcement learning plus reasoning, works surprisingly well across many tasks, so the bottleneck shifts to asking: what should we really be measuring? Some examples would be multi-turn interaction with real users, long-term memory, or tasks where the agent has to keep working over days instead of solving independent episodes. Those are the kinds of environments I find most exciting. They reflect how utility is actually created in the real world, and current setups don't capture that well yet.

So to sum up: real value, the right kind of difficulty, scalable evaluation, and ideally something that challenges our current assumptions about how we evaluate intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response advocates tasks that require important general abilities, but does not say challenging tasks are valuable because they spur fundamentally new methods.

r002.rationale: It contrasts doing well on clean game or synthetic environments with doing useful real-world tasks, and says good tasks should measure abilities that generalize rather than benchmark-specific quirks.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing I look for is whether the task actually matters in the real world. A lot of academic benchmarks are constructed so that they're easy to grade, but they don't correspond to anything a person would actually want done. When I worked on WebShop, the question was, can an agent go to an e-commerce site and buy something you describe in natural language? That's a thing people do every day. SWE-bench is the same idea for software engineering. If you solve the task, you've produced something useful, and that gives you a much better signal than a toy puzzle.

The second thing is that the environment has to be rich enough that reasoning and acting become intertwined. In a pure question answering setting, the model just thinks and then answers. In a good agent environment, the model has to take an action, observe what comes back, and update its plan. That feedback loop is where the interesting behavior shows up. ReAct was really about making that loop explicit, and you can only study it if the environment pushes back on you.

Third, I care about scalability and diversity of the task distribution. If there are only fifty tasks, people will overfit, and you'll learn nothing. You want a space where you can generate many tasks, ideally with automatic verification, so you can also use it for training and not just evaluation. That's become much more important now that reinforcement learning on agents actually works.

And then there's a softer criterion. I like environments that expose a capability gap that is clearly about the agent, not about the base model's knowledge. If a task fails because the model doesn't know some fact, that's not very interesting to me. If it fails because the model couldn't recover from a mistake, couldn't manage a long horizon, or couldn't decide when to explore versus commit, that's a real research problem, and it's the kind of thing I want the environment to isolate.

r001.rationale: The response values real-world usefulness, feedback loops, scalability, and agent capability gaps, but does not say that sufficiently challenging tasks are chosen to spur fundamentally new methods.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss mastering a closed game environment such as Zork or contrast that with abilities that transfer to other tasks.

astra-6.text:
For me, the key question is whether the task actually requires an agent. Does it need to take actions, observe what happens, and adjust its plan? If you can solve it with a single language-model call, it may be a useful task, but it doesn’t tell us much about agent behavior.

I also look for meaningful feedback and a clear way to evaluate success. An agent can produce a very convincing explanation while failing to accomplish the goal. So I’d like the environment to let us check what actually changed, rather than just judge how good the final response sounds.

And I like tasks that are simple enough to study but rich enough to expose interesting failures. When something goes wrong, can we understand whether the problem was reasoning, taking the wrong action, or failing to use feedback? That makes the environment useful for improving agents, beyond just giving them a score.

r001.rationale: The response values tasks that reveal agent failures and support improvement, but does not say challenging research tasks should spur fundamentally new methods.

r002.rationale: The response does not distinguish mastering a closed game such as Zork through reinforcement learning from developing abilities that transfer to other tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I look for tasks where an agent has to interact with an environment over multiple steps, rather than just produce one answer. It takes an action, gets an observation, and then has to decide what to do next. That gives you a way to study planning, reasoning, and learning from feedback together.

I also care about whether success is meaningful and measurable. Can we tell that the agent actually accomplished the goal? And does accomplishing it require something beyond exploiting a narrow benchmark? Ideally, the environment is simple enough that we can understand failures, but rich enough that improving on it teaches us something useful about agents more generally.

r001.rationale: The response says a rich environment can teach us something useful about agents generally, but does not identify spur to fundamentally new methods as a reason to choose sufficiently challenging tasks.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts narrow benchmark exploitation with broader usefulness, but does not clearly distinguish mastering a closed game through reinforcement learning from acquiring abilities that transfer to other tasks.
